lines: My jokes are like my cuts: better when nobody <bold>rushes me</bold>.
Butchery jokes need timing. Mine usually arrive with salt on them.
I keep a spare joke near the smokehouse. It is not always ready for public use.
I told a joke at the smoker once. The workstation took it better than the villagers did.
People say I work too much. I say the work is the only one here that listens.
If confidence could be traded, this village would be rich and still somehow underprepared.
I tried taking a day off. The village immediately treated it like an emergency drill.
A good joke needs timing. Around here, timing usually trips over a chicken.
I would laugh louder, but someone would ask me to explain it and ruin everything.
The bell has one joke. It screams, and everyone suddenly remembers they have legs.
Butcher jokes work best when they are well seasoned.
I had a cutting joke, but it went too far.
My smokehouse joke takes hours and still comes out dry.
I told a sausage joke once. It had links to several others.
A good ham joke should not be overdone.
I tried to tell a cleaver joke, but it split the room.
The stew laughed at me first. That is never a good sign.
I know a joke about salt, but it needs a pinch of courage.
A roast joke is only funny if nobody gets burned.
My best joke is smoked, cured, and still somehow undercooked.
I asked the table for a laugh. It was wooden about it.
Meat puns are rare, unless I cook them longer.
The knife has a sharp sense of humor and poor timing.
I made a joke for market day, but someone traded it for jerky.
The smokehouse tells slow jokes. You smell the punchline later.
